technique_name: HPC-Coder: domain fine-tuning of PolyCoder on a curated HPC/scientific C/C++ source dataset
tools: g++ -O2 -std=c++17 -fopenmp; OpenMPI mpicxx; HuggingFace Trainer with DeepSpeed ZeRO
metrics: efficiency: speedup of generated parallel code over hand-written sequential baselines [execution]; correctness: average pass@k (k=1,10,100) and build rate [execution]; OpenMP pragma accuracy (textual and functional) [similarity-to-reference]
benchmarks: custom HPC code generation benchmark of 25 C/C++ problems (sequential, OpenMP, MPI variants); OpenMP pragma dataset (13,900 samples); relative performance prediction datasets (Kripke/Laghos 830 commits; CodeContests C++ pairs)
models: PolyCoder 2.7B, open, code-specialized base; GPT-Neo 2.7B, open, base; GPT-2 1.5B, open, base (all fine-tuned on HPC data)
baselines: PolyCoder (not fine-tuned); GPT-Neo+HPC; GPT-2+HPC
effect_correctness_headline: can pass these at up to 53% higher rate than the other models (HPC code generation tests)
notes: Efficiency evidence is only Fig. 10: speedups of PolyCoder+HPC generated code over sequential baselines (values in garbled figure roughly 1.5-2.8 for axpy/average/reduce/matmul/fft/cholesky), with no comparison against the base model, so direction for the technique is NR. Main outcomes are correctness (pass@k, build rate). Paper also has non-generation tasks (relative performance classification). Inclusion is borderline under IC3/EC5; reviewer should decide. Figures garbled.

title: RTLLM: An Open-Source Benchmark for Design RTL Generation with Large Language Model
authors: Yao Lu; Shang Liu; Qi-Jun Zhang; Zhiyao Xie
venue: Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference
technique_name: Self-planning (two-step prompting: LLM first produces reasoning steps and syntax-error-avoidance advice, then generates RTL conditioned on them)
tools: Synopsys Design Compiler (compile_ultra) for synthesis and PPA; Synopsys VCS for RTL simulation
iterations: two queries per generation (plan, then code); five independent samples per design; no repair
metrics: efficiency (hardware design quality): area (um^2), power (uW), timing as worst negative slack (ns) of post-synthesis netlist, summarized as count of designs where a method achieves best PPA among correct candidates [tool-static, synthesis]; correctness: syntax (synthesizable, out of 5 samples) and functionality (passes testbench, success if any of 5 passes) [execution]
benchmarks: RTLLM (30 designs: 11 arithmetic, 19 logic), introduced in this paper
models: GPT-3.5, closed, instruct; GPT-4, closed, instruct; Thakur et al. fine-tuned CodeGen 16B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder 15B, open, code-specialized
baselines: Same model without self-planning (GPT-3.5, GPT-4); Thakur et al. fine-tuned model; StarCoder; human designer reference RTL for PPA
effect_correctness_headline: GPT-3.5 alone degrades to 55% correct syntax and 10/30 correct functionalities. After using our self-planning together with GPT-3.5, the performance rise back to 73% and 14/30 (GPT-4.0 + SP: 90%, 19/30 vs GPT-4 81%, 15/30)
notes: Primary contribution is a benchmark; self-planning targets correctness, PPA is a measured co-outcome (treated as efficiency for hardware). PPA headline: Best Quality Num (area, power, timing) GPT-3.5 = 2, 2, 5 vs GPT-3.5 + self-planning = 5, 7, 5 ('GPT-3.5 + self-planning ranks second, with 5, 7, 5 designs achieving the best area, power, and timing'); GPT-4 = 8, 5, 6; GPT-4 + SP PPA not reported in Table IV. The best-count comparison is confounded by functional correctness (only correct designs eligible) and authors call it 'less rigorous'. Tables III/IV heavily garbled in extraction. Venue per metadata ASP-DAC (not stated in the text, arXiv v3). Reviewer should decide whether hardware PPA counts as an NF efficiency outcome.

title: GPT4AIGChip: Towards Next-Generation AI Accelerator Design Automation via Large Language Models
authors: Yonggan Fu; Yong-An Zhang; Zhongzhi Yu; Sixu Li; Zhi-Fan Ye; Chao-Jian Li
venue: 2023 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer Aided Design (ICCAD)
technique_name: GPT4AIGChip: LLM-friendly decoupled HLS template + demo-augmented prompt generator (LLM-selected similar demonstrations) + evolutionary design search with synthesis/performance feedback and code correction
tools: Vivado/Vitis HLS (synthesis, performance and resource estimation); custom error parser; ZCU104 FPGA (XCZU7EV MPSoC) with PYNQ for on-board measurement
iterations: Evolutionary tournament-selection search until a maximum number of cycles; best-performing design chosen
metrics: efficiency: on-board latency of generated accelerators, latency-DSP Pareto frontier [execution]; correctness: Pass@k (successful compilation) and testbench output check [execution]
benchmarks: GEMM-based accelerator design space; six networks (e.g., VGG-16, ResNet-18, W-ResNet-32, ResNet-50) at two resolutions (32x32 CIFAR, 224x224 ImageNet); inner-product HLS task for Pass@100; output-stationary computing unit for Pass@10 ablations
models: GPT-4, size undisclosed, closed, instruct; CodeGen (size not stated), open, code-specialized (base and fine-tuned on HLS)
baselines: CHaiDNN (industry design automation tool); manual expert-optimized designs; random search; prompt ablations (No Demo, High-Level Description, Random/Dissimilar demos, 0-3 demos); CodeGen with/without fine-tuning
effect_target_headline: a 2.0%∼16.0% latency reduction across six networks and two resolution settings (vs CHaiDNN)
effect_correctness_headline: demo-augmented prompt Pass@10 60% vs 10% (No Demo) and 30% (High-Level Description)
notes: Efficiency results are in figures (Fig. 6, 7) and compared to a non-LLM tool and human experts; no LLM no-technique efficiency baseline (prompt ablations are on Pass@10 only). Human intervention still required to fix module interfaces and assemble the accelerator. Pass@k defined as successful compilations. Limitations section present; no explicit threats-to-validity section. Eligibility borderline (HLS hardware code).

title: Enhancing Genetic Improvement Mutations Using Large Language Models
authors: Alexander E. I. Brownlee; James Callan; Karine Even-Mendoza; Alina Geiger; Carol Hanna; Justyna Petke
venue: International Symposium on Search Based Software Engineering
technique_name: LLM-based mutation operator for Genetic Improvement (Gin) with Simple/Medium/Detailed prompts, used in random sampling and local search
tools: Gin GI toolkit (llm branch, commit 9fe9bdf); Gin profiler (20 repeats for hot methods); JavaParser; Langchain4J; JCodec unit tests with 10000 ms timeout
iterations: Random sampling: 1000 edits per type; local search: 10 runs (one per top-10 hot method) of 100 evaluations each (99 edits); LLM asked for 5 variants per request
metrics: efficiency: number of runtime-improving patches, best and median runtime improvement in ms [execution]; correctness: patches parsed (valid), compiled, passed all unit tests [execution]
benchmarks: JCodec (Java), top-10 profiled hot methods
models: GPT-3.5 Turbo, size NR, closed, instruct (temperature 0.7)
baselines: Standard GI Statement edits (copy/delete/replace/swap) and Insert edits (break/continue/return)
effect_target_headline: Medium and Detailed, we found 164 and 196 improvements, respectively, while we only found 136 with Insert and 71 with Statement. The best improvement could be found with 508 ms with the Statement edit. The best improvement found using LLMs (using the Medium prompt) was only able to improve the runtime by 395 ms. (Local Search)
effect_correctness_headline: the number of patches passing unit tests is up to 75% higher for LLM-based edits than GI Insert edits (Random Sampling, Medium prompt: 292 vs 166 passed)
notes: Short paper (~6 pages); metadata venue is International Symposium on Search Based Software Engineering (SSBSE), not stated in the arXiv text. Budget expressed as evaluations (1000 per arm) rather than tokens/cost. Simple prompt yielded 0 passing patches in random sampling. No repeated runs or statistical tests. Also at github.com/gintool/gin llm branch.

title: Advanced Large Language Model (LLM)-Driven Verilog Development: Enhancing Power, Performance, and Area Optimization in Code Synthesis
authors: Kiran Thorat; Jiahui Zhao; Yao-Tian Liu; Hongwu Peng; Xi Xie; Bin Lei
technique_name: VeriPPA: two-stage refinement (VeriRectify simulator error feedback for syntax/functionality, then PPA-constraint prompt with synthesis report feedback and in-context optimization strategy examples)
tools: ICARUS Verilog (iverilog) simulator; Synopsys Design Compiler (compile_ultra) with ASAP 7nm Predictive PDK; Python timing-constraint sweep
iterations: VeriRectify up to K=4 correction attempts, stop when no errors; PPA loop feeds synthesis report back to VeriRectify until PPA goal met (max not stated); 5 generations per design
metrics: efficiency: clock period (ps), power (uW), area (um2) from logic synthesis [tool-static synthesis reports]; correctness: syntax and functionality pass rates via testbench simulation [execution]
benchmarks: RTLLM (29 designs); VerilogEval-Human (156); VerilogEval-Machine (108); PPA optimization shown on 5 selected RTLLM designs
models: GPT-3.5 (closed, instruct); GPT-4 and GPT-4-0314 (closed, instruct); GPT-4 4-shot
baselines: RTLLM (self-planning prompt), VerilogEval, plain GPT-3.5/GPT-4 without correction; non-optimized PPA results as before-state
effect_target_headline: adder 32bit operates at an improved 180ps clock (from 500ps; Power 14.72 uW -> 587.31 uW, Area 213.21 um -> 1005.67 um)
effect_correctness_headline: Our framework achieves 62.0% (+16%) for functional accuracy and 81.37% (+8.3%) for syntactic correctness in Verilog code generation, compared to SOTAs
notes: Scope borderline: NF outcome is hardware PPA of synthesized LLM-generated Verilog, treated as efficiency. PPA optimization results are anecdotal (Table 2: 5 hand-selected designs, only optimized values; before-values shown only for adder_32bit); no systematic PPA comparison with baselines. Claimed 'open-source' but no URL given. Tables 1 and 2 garbled in extraction. No threats/limitations section.

title: MoTCoder: Elevating Large Language Models with Modular of Thought for Challenging Programming Tasks
authors: Jingyao Li; Peng-Guang Chen; Bin Xia; Hong Xu; Jia-Ya Jia
technique_name: Module-of-Thought (MoT) instruction tuning (GPT-4o-transformed modular solutions with sub-module headers/docstrings, plus 'clean' renamed/commented code, filtered by tests)
tools: radon (maintainability index); GPT-4o for data transformation; DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 3
metrics: readability-maintainability: Maintainability Index (Halstead volume, cyclomatic complexity, LOC, comment density) via radon on passing code [tool-static]; efficiency: average execution time (s) and memory usage (MB) on passing samples [execution]; correctness: pass@1 [execution]
benchmarks: APPS test set (introductory/interview/competition); CodeContests test and validation; training data from APPS and CodeContests train (183K clean + 174K MoT samples)
models: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, 7B, open, code-specialized instruct (base for MoTCoder-7B); Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, 32B, open, code-specialized instruct (base for MoTCoder-32B)
baselines: Base Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct; normal fine-tuning on original training solutions; many prior code LLMs (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, WizardCoder, StarCoder, GPT-4o) and code-revision methods (Self-edit, CodeRL, Self-repair, CodeChain)
effect_correctness_headline: APPS pass@1 All: MoTCoder-7B 34.67 vs Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct-7B 32.21 (normal finetuning 27.70); MoTCoder-32B 45.95 vs 40.13; CodeContests All: MoTCoder-7B 19.09, MoTCoder-32B 23.85
notes: Maintainability index and time/memory results are only shown in Figure 4 (b,c) with no printed numbers, so no exact NF headline can be copied; text states MoT code has 'significantly higher maintainability' than normal finetuning and baseline, and 'significantly lower memory consumption' with comparable time. NF metrics computed only on passing code (selection bias). Efficiency effect: memory lower, time comparable. Abstract pass@1 gains (5.8% APPS, 5.9% CodeContests) are relative to prior SOTA. Deduplication between CodeContests train and APPS test reported. No variance, no threats section, no compute reported. Text claims 'MoTCoder-6.7B outperformed GPT-4 by 12.61%' appears inconsistent with the current tables (stale from earlier version).

title: BetterV: Controlled Verilog Generation with Discriminative Guidance
authors: Ze-Hua Pei; Hui-Ling Zhen; M. Yuan; Yu Huang; Bei Yu
technique_name: BetterV: domain-specific instruct-tuning (Verilog-C alignment, autocompletion, data augmentation) + task-specific generative discriminator guiding decoding via Bayes-rule weighted decoding
tools: Yosys (proc; aigmap; stat for AIG node counts; sat -verify -seq 100 -tempinduct -prove-asserts for SAT runtime; eqy equivalence checking; prep for syntax); V2C Verilog-to-C translator; DeepSpeed ZeRO, LoRA, DeepSpeed-Chat
metrics: efficiency: synthesized And-Inverter-Graph netlist node count (area proxy) [tool-static]; SAT formal-verification solving time [execution]; correctness: pass@k functional correctness via simulation, syntactic correctness via Yosys compilation [execution]
benchmarks: VerilogEval (machine and human subsets); 18 VerilogEval-human problems for node reduction; 5 designs from ANSI-C hardware verification benchmarks for SAT runtime
models: CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; CodeQwen1.5-7B-Chat, open, code-specialized; discriminators: TinyLlama, open, base; DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized
baselines: BetterV-base (instruct-tuned without discriminator); reference Verilog; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, CodeQwen, ChipNeMo, Thakur et al., VerilogEval, RTLCoder (correctness)
effect_target_headline: on average, the Verilog generated by BetterV have 46.52% fewer nodes than the reference model and 31.68% less nodes than BetterV-base; can save 22.45% in verification time compared with the reference Verilog, and 13.99% in time compared with BetterV-base
effect_correctness_headline: BetterV-CodeQwen ... pass@1 on VerilogEval-machine and VerilogEval-human outperforms GPT-4 by 8.1 and 2.6, respectively
notes: NF dimension mapping is a judgement call: AIG node count (circuit area/PPA) and SAT verification runtime coded as efficiency. NF experiments use only BetterV-CodeLlama on a small selection of problems (18 and 5); correctness of the node-reduced rewrites is not reported for those tasks. Rewrite task (from a reference module) for NF experiments rather than generation from scratch. Hyperparameters lambda, w, rho, tau are task-sensitive and not given. Limitations section brief; no threats to validity; no code URL.

title: Make Every Move Count: LLM-based High-Quality RTL Code Generation Using MCTS
authors: Matthew DeLorenzo; A. B. Chowdhury; Vasudev Gohil; Shailja Thakur; Ramesh Karri; Siddharth Garg
technique_name: VeriGen+MCTS (Monte Carlo tree-search decoding with compile/function/PPA reward, comment-token pruning, modular reuse of submodules)
tools: Icarus Verilog 10.3 (compilability/functional check); custom Yosys scripts for synthesis to obtain area and delay
iterations: MCTS iterations per module (up to ~300 shown); reward alpha_NC=-1, alpha_NF=-0.1, alpha_B=0.5; no explicit stopping rule beyond iteration budget
metrics: efficiency: area-delay product (ADP), area (um2), delay (ps) from Yosys synthesis (tool-static/synthesis); correctness: functional correctness per module via simulation testbench (execution)
benchmarks: Custom set of 15 Verilog problems (adders, multipliers, MAC units at 4/8/16/32/64 bits)
models: VeriGen-2B (CodeGen fine-tuned on Verilog), open, code-specialized
baselines: Vanilla VeriGen greedy decoding; VeriGen + beam search
effect_target_headline: For the largest design generated by the state-of-the-art LLM (16-bit adder), our technique can achieve a 31.8% improvement in the area-delay product.
effect_correctness_headline: VeriGen+MCTS produces functionally correct codes for all tested modules (15/15), whereas VeriGen and VeriGen+Beam Search fail for 14 and 11 of the 15 tested modules
notes: NF outcome is hardware PPA (ADP) of LLM-generated Verilog, mapped to efficiency. ADP comparison possible only for few modules (4-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit adders, 16-bit multiplier) since baselines rarely produce functional code; average ADP improvement 5.69% over VeriGen and 14.27% over beam search. Single model (VeriGen-2B chosen for runtime). Compute reported as MCTS iteration rate per minute. Table 3 garbled.

title: Comparing Large Language Models and Human Programmers for Generating Programming Code
authors: Wenpin Hou; Zhicheng Ji

models: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0613, closed, instruct) for optimization; generation comparison also includes GPT-3.5-turbo-0613, Gemini Ultra 1.0, Gemini Pro, Claude 2, Llama 2 70B, Code Llama 34B

title: VERT: Verified Equivalent Rust Transpilation with Large Language Models as Few-Shot Learners
authors: Aidan Z. H. Yang; Yoshiki Takashima; Brandon Paulsen; Josiah Dodds; Daniel Kroening
technique_name: VERT (LLM transpilation to safe Rust + rustc error-guided rule-based repair + few-shot re-prompting with equivalence-check counterexamples against an rWasm oracle)
tools: rustc (error-message-guided repair); WebAssembly compilers + rWasm (oracle); bolero (property-based testing); Kani bounded model checker; Verus (manual verification); Clippy (linter, evaluation); rustfmt (formatting before LoC count)
iterations: Re-prompt the LLM up to 20 times; rustc helper-message repairs applied first; stop when equivalence check (PBT, then bounded, then full verification, 120 s limit each) succeeds
metrics: readability-maintainability: Clippy warnings per function [tool-static]; lines of code after rustfmt [tool-static]; correctness: compiled, property-based testing pass, bounded verification pass, full verification pass [execution / formal verification]
benchmarks: TransCoder-IR benchmark subset: 569 C++, 520 C (506 stated elsewhere), 341 Go programs; 14 pointer-manipulating C programs from C2Rust/Laertes/CROWN projects (used for safe-Rust and readability/idiomaticity evaluation)
models: TransCoder-IR (open, translation-specialized, baseline); CodeLlama-2 13B (open, code-specialized); StarCoder 15.5B fine-tuned with adapter layers on 94 LeetCode solutions (open, code-specialized); Anthropic Claude-2 ~130B (closed, instruct)
baselines: TransCoder-IR single-shot; LLM single-shot; few-shot repair without counterexamples (ablation); for readability/idiomaticity: rule-based CROWN and rWasm transpilers
effect_target_headline: On average, Clippy produces 10.9 warnings per function for CROWN, and 372 warnings per function for rWasm. Clippy does not produce any warnings on VERT's transpilations (14 C pointer programs); VERT produces 5X less LoC than CROWN, 10x less LoC than rWasm
effect_correctness_headline: Combining Anthropic's Claude-2 and VERT increases Rust transpilations passing property-based testing from 31% to 54% and bounded model-checking from 1% to 42% compared to using Claude alone.
notes: Main goal is verified correctness; readability/idiomaticity (Clippy, LoC) is reported only for Claude-2 VERT outputs on the 14 C programs and compared with rule-based transpilers, not with the LLM alone, so the NF gain attributable to the loop itself is not isolated. The prompt asks for safe Rust and outputs are filtered for safe Rust (memory safety), but no quantitative security comparison is given. Wilcoxon signed-rank test reported for correctness only (p 1e-5 to 4e-5). Table 1 is flattened in the extraction but readable. C benchmark count inconsistent (506 vs 520). Claude-2 cost $0.0465 per thousand tokens stated; per-component runtimes in Table 2.

title: Time to Separate from StackOverflow and Match with ChatGPT for Encryption
authors: Ehsan Firouzi; Mohammad Ghafari
technique_name: Security-explicit prompting (ask ChatGPT to provide a 'secure' solution/code example)
metrics: security: number of answers free of violations of 13 symmetric-encryption crypto-misuse rules mapped to CWE-327/798/330/326/259, judged manually by two raters with a third as tie-breaker (Cohen's k = 0.82) [human]
benchmarks: 100 StackOverflow JCA symmetric-encryption questions with accepted answers, each containing at least one security violation (sampled from 400 manually inspected posts; Stack Exchange dump of March 8, 2023)
models: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), closed, instruct
baselines: Exact StackOverflow question prompt ('answer this StackOverflow question and provide a code example'): only 3 of 100 responses free of violations
effect_target_headline: When we explicitly prompted to provide a “secure solution”, it cleared violations in 42 questions.
human_eval_details: Two authors (A1, A2) independently inspected ChatGPT answers against 13 security rules; third rater (A3) for persistent disagreements; Cohen's k = 0.82
notes: Borderline eligibility: the paper is mainly an empirical study of StackOverflow posts (RQ1, RQ2); the LLM part (RQ3) is a small evaluation of prompting strategies on 100 questions with a single model. Correctness/completeness was judged only for answers to the exact-question prompt (67 of 100 as good as accepted answers), not for the secure-prompt outputs. Remaining 32 posts insecure mainly due to CBC mode. Additional prompt variants (security guidelines in prompt, 'secure example for production') reported qualitatively. No repeated runs; ChatGPT answers noted to change over time.

title: LLM-Vectorizer: LLM-Based Verified Loop Vectorizer
authors: Jubi Taneja; Avery Laird; Cong Yan; M. Musuvathi; Shuvendu K. Lahiri
venue: IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization
technique_name: LLM-Vectorizer (multi-agent finite-state-machine with Clang dependence-analysis input, checksum-based test feedback, and Alive2 bounded translation validation)
tools: Clang dependence analysis (Clang-19.0.0); checksum-based testing; Alive2 with Z3 (plus C-level unrolling and spatial case splitting); GCC-10.5.0, Clang-19.0.0, ICC-2021.10.0 for performance comparison
iterations: up to ten attempts or until a plausible (checksum-equivalent) solution is found; max observed 7
metrics: efficiency: runtime speedup vs GCC/Clang/ICC auto-vectorized code [execution]; correctness: checksum-based plausibility, pass@k, Alive2 formal equivalence (bounded) [execution / formal verification]
benchmarks: TSVC (Test Suite for Vectorizing Compilers), 149 integer for-loops
models: GPT-4 (API 2023-08-01-preview), closed, general instruct
baselines: GCC-10.5.0, Clang-19.0.0, ICC-2021.10.0 auto-vectorization (efficiency); GPT-4 single/multiple code completions without agents (correctness)
effect_target_headline: run-time speedup ranging from 1.1x to 9.4x as compared to the state-of-the-art compilers such as Intel Compiler, GCC, and Clang (57 formally verified TSVC tests)
effect_correctness_headline: the total number of plausible tests increased to 96 when considering just one LLM invocation, compared to the initial 72 tests; formally verify ... 57 (38.2%) of the test programs
notes: Speedup figure (Figure 6) not extractable; text notes slowdowns vs compilers in several categories (naively vectorizable, reduction), so efficiency effect is positive overall but not uniform. Efficiency is compared to compilers, not to GPT-4 without the agent loop; the agent FSM itself is evaluated only on correctness/LLM invocations. Input is existing scalar code (source-to-source optimization), so a reviewer may consider it adjacent. Only one model (GPT-4), no repeated runs or threats section.

title: Code-Optimise: Self-Generated Preference Data for Correctness and Efficiency
authors: Leonidas Gee; Milan Gritta; Gerasimos Lampouras; I. Iacobacci
venue: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
technique_name: Code-Optimise (self-generated preference data; DPO QvS/PvF/All and SFT top-N% with Dynamic Solution Selection)
tools: Python interpreter + custom timing module (each solution executed 50 times, repeated until CoV <= 0.1, up to 1K times; averaged over 5 runs)
metrics: efficiency: median runtime (ns) of working solutions on the common solved subset [execution]; also Best@100 runtime [execution]; code length in characters (inference cost) [tool-static]; correctness: pass@1/10/100
benchmarks: MBPP (train/validation for training, test split in-domain); HumanEval (164 problems, out-of-domain)
models: StarCoder-1B (open, code-specialized base); StarCoder-3B (open, code-specialized base); CodeLlama-7B (open, code-specialized base); CodeLlama-13B (open, code-specialized base)
baselines: Base pretrained CLM (no fine-tuning); SFT25 and SFT100; static vs dynamic solution selection ablation
effect_target_headline: decreasing the competitive baseline runtimes by an additional 6% for in-domain data and up to 3% for out-of-domain data (DPO QvS / DPO All, averaged across model sizes)
effect_correctness_headline: CodeLlama-13B MBPP pass@1: Base 23.70 vs DPO QvS 33.50 vs DPO PvF 34.10
notes: Runtime effects are modest and inconsistent across models (e.g. DPO All slower on StarCoder-1B HumanEval; HumanEval runtimes less predictable); SFT generally increases runtime. Code length reductions (up to 48% MBPP / 23% HumanEval) framed as inference-cost savings, not readability. Variance reported as CoV of runtime only; no significance tests. Limitations section is brief. Tables extracted cleanly in appendix.

title: Efficacy of Various Large Language Models in Generating Smart Contracts
authors: Siddhartha Chatterjee; B. Ramamurthy
technique_name: Structured (pseudo-code style) prompting versus descriptive natural-language prompting for smart contract generation
tools: HardHat (Web3/Ethereum development environment) for compilation and test execution; TypeScript test files written by the authors; Solidity 0.8.20; no versions given for HardHat or the Solidity compiler; no static analyzer or security scanner was used
iterations: None; single-shot generation per model per prompt per contract, no refinement loop
metrics: efficiency: 'execution efficiency' reported as whole-second execution time for the contract's test run [execution]. readability-maintainability: 'quality/verboseness' reported as free-text qualitative labels such as 'Excellent', 'Unnecessary variable check', 'No SPDX license identifier (warning flag)', 'Extra unspecified parameter', 'Majority code is excellent but few syntax errors' [human, single unblinded rater, no agreement reported]. security: qualitative observations only, e.g. a missing check that unlockTime must exceed the initialization time [human]. Correctness: accuracy as the percentage of author-written test cases passed [execution]

models: GPT 4; GPT 4-o; GPT 3.5; Cohere (Coral); Mistral; Claude; Gemini (Gemini Pro) - all closed or hosted instruct models; exact versions, dates and decoding settings not reported. 'Bard' also appears in the per-case observations but is not a column in any results table

effect_target_headline: Execution efficiency was essentially flat across both strategies: Storage was 2s for all seven models under both text-based (Table 2) and structured (Table 5) prompting; for Lock, GPT 4 went from 2s (text-based) to 3s (structured), Cohere was 3s under both, Claude 3s (text-based) and N/A (structured), Gemini 2s (text-based) and N/A (structured). All 'Create a New Token' efficiency cells are N/A under both strategies. Qualitatively: 'The efficiency of the programs is noticeably slow currently' and 'Code was also rather inefficient compared to human-written equivalent contracts', neither quantified
effect_correctness_headline: Structured prompting lowered test-pass accuracy on the Lock task for several models: Claude 100% (text-based, Table 1) versus 0% (structured, Table 4); Gemini 89% versus N/A; Cohere 78% versus 89%; GPT 4 89% under both; GPT 4-o 100% under both; GPT 3.5 0% under both. All seven models scored 100% on Storage under both strategies and N/A on Create a New Token under both. 'foundational models generally performed better using descriptive prompting as opposed to structured prompting'
human_eval_details: The code-quality column (Tables 3 and 6) is an unstructured qualitative judgement by the authors; the number of raters is not stated and no inter-rater agreement is reported
notes: Substantial quality concerns a human reviewer should weigh. (1) ELIGIBILITY IS BORDERLINE: the paper is mostly a cross-model benchmarking study (which would be the 'context' side list), and only Section 4.3 plus the paired result tables make it a prompting-technique comparison; the only quantitative non-functional outcome is a whole-second execution time that is identical (2s) for nearly every model and task, so a reviewer could reasonably exclude under EC5 or route it to 'context'. Gas cost, the natural efficiency metric for smart contracts, is discussed in the conclusion but never measured. (2) Only three tasks with one generation per model per prompt; no repeats, no variance, no statistical test. (3) Every 'Create a New Token' cell in all six tables is N/A, so the most complex task yields no data at all. (4) Internal inconsistencies: the descriptive prompt in Section 3.3 asks for an ERC-20 token while the structured prompt specifies ERC 721 and the conclusion refers to ERC-721; the Overall Findings cite 'Table 2 & Table 5' (the efficiency tables) when discussing accuracy, which should almost certainly be Tables 1 and 4; 'Bard' appears in the per-case observations and in finding 5 but is not a column in any table, while 'Gemini' is; finding 5 attributes the unlockTime vulnerability to 'Bard and GPT 4-o' whereas Section 3.2 attributes it to 'GPT-4 and Bard'; the Future Work section claims 'moving to more structured prompts significantly improves the quality and efficiency', directly contradicting the paper's own Section 4.3 and results. (5) Mistral's Lock result is N/A in the accuracy table but Table 3 records 'Did not compile', so N/A conflates several failure modes. (6) No security tooling (no Slither, Mythril, or similar) was used despite security being a headline claim; security findings are anecdotal. (7) No artifact, no code or test files released, no model versions or decoding parameters, no threats-to-validity section, no contamination discussion (notably relevant since the Lock contract is HardHat's own tutorial example and is near-certainly in the training data). (8) The extracted text is full of soft-hyphen/control characters and the six tables are heavily garbled, with headers separated from values; the mappings above were reconstructed from the column order and cross-checked against the running text, but should be verified against the original PDF.

title: Project-Level C-to-Rust Translation via Pointer Knowledge Graphs
authors: Zhiqiang Yuan; Wenjun Mao; Zhuo-Fu Chen; Xiaotang Shang; Chong Wang; Yiling Lou

title: AccelOpt: A Self-Improving LLM Agentic System for AI Accelerator Kernel Optimization

notes: Dimension mapping is a judgment call a human reviewer should confirm: the paper's 'safety' metrics (raw pointer declarations/dereferences, pointer arithmetic/comparisons, unsafe lines/casts/calls) are memory-safety proxies and were coded as the security dimension, while 'idiomaticity' (Clippy flags per normalized KLoC) and the three readability metrics were coded as readability-maintainability. Tables 1, 2 and 3 and Figures 6, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 14 are badly garbled by PDF extraction (column values appear as long interleaved runs of numbers), so only the aggregate figures quoted in the running text were copied; per-project values must be re-checked against the PDF. The paper also reports a human study, but it measures repair effort rather than rating code quality: one developer with over ten years of C and Rust experience and no familiarity with the subjects repaired the non-equivalent translations in 4.5 hours on average (min 0.33, max 10), with a strong size-effort correlation (rho = 0.86, p = 1.59e-4); there is a single annotator and no agreement statistic, which is why human_eval is coded 'none'. Statistical tests are reported only for effort/cost/time correlations, not for the quality metrics, and each project appears to be translated once with no repeated runs or variance. The reported 87% functional equivalence is not fully automated. Contamination of the open-source C subjects in the models' pretraining is never discussed. A_max and the block threshold theta_b are not given numerically (theta_f is 50% of the LLM context window). The authors note they recalculated several baselines' metrics after finding bugs or suppressed Clippy rules in those artifacts, which makes the baseline numbers theirs rather than as-published.

title: His2Trans: A Knowledge-Guided Agentic Framework for Project-Level C-to-Rust Migration
authors: Sheng-Bo Wang; Ming-Wei Liu; Guang-Sheng Ou; Yuwen Chen; Zi-Ke Li; Yan-Lin Wang
technique_name: His2Trans (historical C/Rust migration knowledge mining and retrieval at interface and fragment level, scaffold-constrained knowledge-guided function translation, then project-level agentic refinement with compilation, semantic and unsafe feedback)
tools: Clang 14.0.0; Rust 1.94.0-nightly; Python 3.13.5; jina-reranker-v3 style neural reranker for mining C/Rust pairs; project build systems (GN/Ninja for OpenHarmony); Ubuntu 22.04, dual Intel Xeon Gold 6430, 503 GiB RAM, 4x NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada
iterations: Refinement agent iterates within a fixed budget (budget value not stated); per-function translation retries on validation failure; translation ordered by scaffold dependency graph
metrics: security/memory-safety: Unsafe Ratio = fraction of Rust source lines inside or directly associated with unsafe constructs [tool-static]; correctness: Incremental Compilation Pass Rate (per-function body replay under a common scaffold) and Test Pass Rate on the project's own tests [execution]; all averaged per project then across projects
benchmarks: Two datasets: 10 OpenHarmony modules (161-3,544 LOC each, 1-14 files, 7-160 functions, 4-135 tests) and 8 open-source C projects used in prior C-to-Rust studies (urlparser, avl, ht, qsort, buffer, rgba, quadtree, genann)
models: DeepSeek V4 Pro, size NR, open-weight, instruct (main translation and refinement); Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, 32B, open, code-specialized (offline knowledge extraction only); Claude Code (general coding agent, underlying model not stated) as a baseline
baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpilation); C2SaferRust (unsafe-reduction pipeline); EvoC2Rust; Tymcrat; Claude Code-only (general SE agent); plus an ablation: knowledge-guided translation alone, + compiler-driven per-function repair, + project-level agentic refinement
effect_target_headline: On ten OpenHarmony modules, His2Trans reaches a 100.00% incremental compilation pass rate, a 94.92% Test Pass Rate, and a 16.35% Unsafe Ratio. On eight open-source C projects, it reaches 100.00% for both incremental compilation and Test Pass Rate, reducing Unsafe Ratio from 42.88% under C2Rust to 8.59%
effect_correctness_headline: OpenHarmony averages: Test Pass Rate 94.92% (His2Trans) vs 80.08% (Claude Code-only), 67.50% (C2Rust), 40.92% (C2SaferRust), 0.00% (EvoC2Rust and Tymcrat); incremental compilation 100.00% vs 99.58% for C2Rust
notes: Unsafe Ratio is treated here as the security/memory-safety dimension; a reviewer who reads 'security' strictly as vulnerabilities/CWE may disagree, and unsafe ratio is also partly a maintainability/idiomaticity proxy. The effect direction is not uniformly positive against every baseline: on the open-source dataset Claude Code-only reaches a lower Unsafe Ratio (4.04% vs 8.59%) at equal compilation and test pass rates, which the authors attribute to Claude Code being free to abandon the C-compatible interface boundary; on OpenHarmony His2Trans is clearly better (16.35% vs 33.67%). Ablation on OpenHarmony: knowledge-guided translation alone 95.82% / 39.29% / 15.95% unsafe; + compiler-driven per-function repair 100.00% / 94.92% / 22.52%; + project-level refinement 100.00% / 94.92% / 16.35%, i.e. the refinement stage buys back unsafe reduction without changing test pass rate. The Unsafe Ratio instrument (how lines 'directly associated with' unsafe are counted) is defined only in prose, no tool named. Single translation model, no repeated runs or statistical tests, no token/cost/time reporting. Contamination: evaluated target modules are excluded from the retrieval pool and a threats paragraph acknowledges residual leakage from public mirrors and pretraining data. Tables IV and V are heavily garbled in extraction (per-project columns interleaved); the quoted numbers are taken from the abstract, prose and average rows, which are unambiguous. Venue metadata is empty; arXiv v4 (cs.SE), formatted as an IEEE conference submission.

title: Agent Factories for High Level Synthesis: How Far Can General-Purpose Coding Agents Go in Hardware Optimization?
authors: Abhishek Bhandwaldar; M. Choudhury; Ruchir Puri; Akash Srivastava
technique_name: Agent factory: Stage 1 per-sub-kernel optimizer agents (7 variants each) + agent-formulated ILP selection under area budget; Stage 2 N parallel exploration agents doing cross-function pragma/code/memory/compute optimizations (agent scaling N in {1,2,4,8,10})
tools: AMD Vitis HLS (latency and area reports); ILP solver; ABC logic synthesis for ASIC area correlation; Claude Code agent harness
iterations: Stage 1: M = 7 variants per sub-function; Stage 2: N exploration agents each iteratively refining one top-N ILP solution (stopping rule not specified); correctness-failing variants discarded
metrics: efficiency: latency speedup over baseline from HLS timing reports (tool-static/synthesis estimate), area (HLS-reported resource usage and ABC logic area), Pareto fronts; correctness used only as a filter (functional correctness test vs original design), not reported
benchmarks: 12 HLS kernels: 6 HLS-Eval (AES, DES, KMP, NW, PRESENT, SHA256) and 6 Rodinia-HLS (lavamd, kmeans, hotspot, leukocyte, cfd, streamcluster); 5 runs each
models: Claude Opus 4.5, closed, reasoning; Claude Opus 4.6, closed, reasoning (via Claude Code)
baselines: unoptimized design; bounded exhaustive pragma-only search with ILP selection (HLS-Eval kernels); reference optimized implementations (Rodinia-HLS); agent counts N=1 vs larger N
effect_target_headline: Scaling from 1 to 10 agents yields a mean 7.07× speedup over baseline, with gains concentrated on harder problems: leukocyte and kmeans reaches ∼10×
notes: Eligibility borderline: NF outcome is hardware latency/area of HLS designs produced by LLM edits of existing kernels (could be viewed as adjacent optimization of human-written code). Inconsistent headline numbers: abstract says mean 7.07x, introduction says 8.27x; Table II peak 7.07x at N=8 and 6.53x at N=10; streamcluster stated >20x in intro but ~5-6x in results. Results averaged over 5 runs but no variance shown. Single model family; baselines are bounded pragma-only search, not SOTA DSE (AutoDSE). 'Anonymized implementation' link mentioned but no URL in text. Figures garbled.

title: Improving Efficiency of GPU Kernel Optimization Agents using a Domain-Specific Language and Speed-of-Light Guidance
authors: S. Hari; V. Balaji; S. Damani; Qi-Jing Huang; Christoforos E. Kozyrakis
technique_name: uCUTLASS: compact DSL learned in context, compiled to CUTLASS kernels (with static validation feedback) inside a Measure-Implement generate-compile-test-profile agent loop
tools: uCUTLASS compiler (Lark grammar, static validation, CUTLASS 3.x CollectiveBuilder / CUTLASS Python API cutlass_cppgen); NVIDIA Nsight Compute (ncu); OpenHands agent runtime; NGC container PyTorch 2.10.0a0 + CUDA 13.0; H100 with locked clocks
iterations: 40 generate-compile-test-profile attempts per problem (matched budget across variants)
metrics: efficiency: geomean and median speedup over PyTorch of NCU-profiled kernel time, Fast-p and Attempt-Fast-p(2) curves, signed area between Fast-p curves [execution]; integrity filtering of gaming kernels via SOL-ceiling check, LLM-based game detector and PyTorch-only detector [execution + llm-judge]; correctness: pass of correctness check against PyTorch reference, problems solved [execution]
benchmarks: KernelBench (Levels 1-3), 59-problem LLM-relevant subset
models: GPT-5-mini, size NR, closed, reasoning; GPT-5, size NR, closed, reasoning; GPT-5.2, size NR, closed, reasoning
baselines: Flat Measure-Implement (MI) agent generating raw CUDA/CUTLASS code with same budget; Sakana AI CUDA Engineer archive (Claude 3.5 Sonnet kernels)
effect_target_headline: improving GPT-5-mini from 0.40× to 1.27× (3.2× improvement), GPT-5 from 0.86× to 1.69× (2.0× improvement), and GPT-5.2 from 2.04× to 2.85× (1.4× improvement)
notes: Efficiency here is runtime speedup of LLM-generated GPU kernels; the paper also frames 'efficiency' as iteration/token efficiency of the agent (scheduling saves 19-43% tokens), which is agent cost, not code quality. GPT-5.2 best SOL-guided variant uses in-prompt form; uCUTLASS+SOL on GPT-5.2 (2.79x) does not exceed uCUTLASS alone (2.85x). Correctness reported only as solved counts in text (e.g., MI GPT-5-mini solves 52 of 59), no clean correctness comparison. Results are after integrity filtering (LLM game detector). Stability: one independent repeat run for GPT-5-mini plus ablation envelope, CV reported. Figures not in extracted text; compiler code not released (grammar in appendix). No explicit threats-to-validity section.

title: Kernel-Smith: A Unified Recipe for Evolutionary Kernel Optimization
authors: He Du; Qi-Ming Ge; Jiakai Hu; Aijun Yang; Zheng-Zhou Cai; Zixian Huang
technique_name: Kernel-Smith (evaluation-driven evolutionary kernel agent + step-centric evolution-oriented post-training: SFT cold start and GRPO RL on 'best evolution steps')
tools: OpenEvolve evolutionary coding agent (island model + MAP-Elites archive); custom distributed evaluation service with warm-up runs, repeated measurement with outlier removal and CUDAGraph timing (execution-time fluctuation constrained to within 1%); runtime hack-detection to prevent fallback to native PyTorch ops; Triton backend on NVIDIA GPUs and MACA backend on MetaX GPUs; HDBSCAN clustering for data curation; GRPO for RL. No version numbers given.
iterations: 40 rounds of iterative evolution per model under the unified protocol; input prompt and max output capped at 32K tokens per round; real-world application cases run up to 512 iterations. No early-stopping rule stated.
metrics: efficiency: Average Speedup Ratio (avg AMSR, mean speedup over PyTorch eager baseline with sub-1.0 speedups scored zero) and Fast Proportion (fast_1, fraction of kernels faster than the baseline) [execution]; end-to-end serving latency and throughput for the real-world cases [execution]. correctness: 'corr', numerical agreement with the PyTorch reference within tolerance after hack detection [execution].
benchmarks: KernelBench (Triton backend), Levels 1/2/3 reported separately plus an average; a MetaX MACA benchmark the authors construct of 45 common operators (Activation 15, Normalization 8, Reduction&Aggregation 17, Loss Function 5); three real-world cases (SGLang normal_decode_set_metadata, LMDeploy DeepSeek MoE routing, DeepSeek Engram). Task counts per KernelBench level not restated in the text.
languages: Triton (Python), MACA (MetaX GPU backend), PyTorch/CUDA as reference
models: Kernel-Smith-235B-SFT and Kernel-Smith-235B-RL (trained from Qwen3-235B-A22B, open-weights, reasoning); Kernel-Smith-MACA-30B and Kernel-Smith-MACA-235B (open-weights); baselines Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507-think; Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-think; MiniMax-M2.5; Kimi-K2.5; DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale / DeepSeek-v3.2-think (all open-weights); Gemini-3.0-pro (closed); Claude-4.6-opus (closed); GPT-OSS-20B; Qwen3-30B-A3B. Teacher models for data synthesis: DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale and Gemini-3.0-pro.
baselines: The same Kernel-Smith evolutionary agent framework driven by untrained open-weights and proprietary models (agent held constant); for the RL model, the Qwen3-235B-A22B base model and the SFT-only variant; for kernels, PyTorch eager mode (NVIDIA) and a correctness-verified LLM-generated CUDA implementation (MetaX).
effect_target_headline: "recording the highest avg amsr of 3.70 across all difficulty levels" (Kernel-Smith-235B-RL, KernelBench AVG Level-1/2/3, vs Claude-4.6-opus 3.33 and DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale 3.44); "this distinct advantage is particularly pronounced in the Level 2 subset, where our model delivers a remarkable avg amsr of 7.77, substantially exceeding even Claude-4.6-opus (5.83)"; MACA backend AVG avg AMSR 13.27 (Kernel-Smith-MACA-30B) and 14.26 (Kernel-Smith-MACA-235B) vs 12.30 (Qwen3-235B-2507-think); real-world: "4.78x speedup" (SGLang kernel), "about 1.36x speedup" (LMDeploy routing kernel), "a reported 14.59x speedup" (DeepSeek Engram).
effect_correctness_headline: "achieving an average corr of 96.33 to effectively outperform all other advanced baselines, including Gemini-3.0-pro (94.33) and DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale (94.67)"; Claude-4.6-opus remains higher at 99.33. Level 3 corr 94 for Kernel-Smith-235B-RL.
artifact_url: https://chat.intern-ai.org.cn/kernel-smith (project page / online demo); data access by e-mail request only; merged PRs https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/20778, https://github.com/InternLM/lmdeploy/pull/4345, https://github.com/DeepLink-org/DLBlas/pull/102; agent built on https://github.com/algorithmicsuperintelligence/openevolve
notes: Tables 1 and 2 are badly garbled by PDF extraction (column headers are detached from values); the numbers quoted above were cross-checked against the prose in Sections 5.2-5.3, which states them explicitly, except the MACA AVG column values (13.27/14.26 and the baseline 12.30) which were read off the reconstructed table and should be verified against the original PDF. The agent framework and the post-training recipe are presented as one unified recipe and are not separately ablated against a multi-turn-agent baseline, so they are recorded as a single hybrid technique; an SFT-only variant appears only in the Figure 1 curve, not in Table 1. KernelBench task counts per level are never restated. No threats-to-validity section. Compute is reported as a protocol budget (40 evolution rounds, 32K-token cap per round, 100 repeated unit-test executions) rather than measured cost, hence QA7 = 0.5. Contamination is addressed only indirectly, via the DeepSeek Engram case chosen as a fresh module.

title: CuTeGen: An LLM-Based Agentic Framework for Generation and Optimization of High-Performance GPU Kernels using CuTe
authors: Tara Saba; Zhi-Yang Chen; Jikai Jason Li; Anne Ouyang; Xujie Si; Fan Long
technique_name: CuTeGen (CuTe-targeted generate-test-refine agent with diagnosis/patch repair, category-aware structural optimization prompts and delayed Nsight Compute profiling feedback)
tools: NVIDIA Nsight Compute; PyTorch 2.8.0 CUDA extension interface; CUTLASS v4.3.0 (commit acb4593) / CuTe; CUDA 13.0; RTX 4090
iterations: Correctness loop (diagnosis then localized patch) until correct or max rounds; optimization loop applies one optimization per iteration until max round reached; profiling feedback withheld early for structurally complex kernels (e.g., matmul); exact max rounds not stated
metrics: efficiency: average speedup over PyTorch eager runtime, Fast1 (% tasks faster than PyTorch), speedup on Fast1, % best kernel, low-precision rate [execution]; correctness: % tasks with at least one correct kernel passing automated tests and manual inspection [execution + human audit]
benchmarks: KernelBench Level-1 and Level-2, 209 tasks
models: GPT-5, size undisclosed, closed, reasoning
baselines: PyTorch eager reference; CudaForge (agentic, GPT-5, 10 rounds); ablations: CuTeGen with raw CUDA, without profiling, profiling from start
effect_target_headline: CuTeGen achieves an average speedup of 1.71× over PyTorch vs CudaForge 0.89× (KernelBench L1+L2, 209 tasks, GPT-5)
effect_correctness_headline: Correct 87% (CuTeGen) vs 63% (CudaForge), KernelBench L1+L2
notes: Single model (GPT-5) justified only by compute budget in Limitations. Manual audit excluded reduced-precision kernels from speedups (CudaForge 24% low precision). Cost $1.69 vs $1.41 per task. Per-level tables: L1 1.32x vs 0.61x; L2 2.12x vs 1.19x. Ablation (L1 total speedup): CuTeGen 1.35x vs with cuda 1.12x. No repeated runs/variance. Max iteration counts not given. Tables garbled but recoverable.

title: PAFT: Preservation-Aware Fine-Tuning for Minimal-Edit Program Repair
authors: Bo-Yang Yang; Zi-Jian Cai; Shun-Fu Jin; Hao-Ye Tian
technique_name: PAFT: preservation-aware fine-tuning (token-level alignment-based upweighting of copy-worthy target tokens, full-sequence loss masking, edit-difficulty curriculum) with QLoRA
tools: Ratcliff/Obershelp (SequenceMatcher-style) token alignment between buggy and fixed code; QLoRA 4-bit NF4, rank 32, alpha 16, 3 epochs, w_align = 2.0; single RTX 4090
metrics: readability-maintainability (patch minimality / stable-context preservation on plausible patches): Average Edit Distance (character Levenshtein) [tool-static], Code Consistency Rate [tool-static], Average Total Changed Lines and Tokens [tool-static]; metrics validated by human preference study [human]; correctness: pass@1/5/10 via compilation and test suites [execution]
benchmarks: Defects4J (MORepair release, single-file Java bugs); HumanEval-Java; training on TutorLLMCode (1535 instances)
models: Qwen3-8B (open); OpenCoder-8B-Instruct (open, code-specialized instruct); DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B (open, code-specialized); Qwen3-Max (closed, zero-shot reference); DeepSeek-V3 (open, zero-shot reference)
baselines: Base models; standard SFT (assistant-only masking); minimal-change Prompting; RepairLLaMA; AdaPatcher (SFT + DPO)
effect_target_headline: reducing average edit distance (AED) by up to 32.6% over Sft; Defects4J DS-Coder-6.7B: reduces AED from 142.9 to 80.7, and increases CCR from 70.7 to 76.3; vs AdaPatcher median AED from 61.0 to 42.0
effect_correctness_headline: PAFT improves pass@1 by up to 65.6% over standard supervised fine-tuning (Sft); Defects4J DS-Coder-6.7B pass@1 from 5.8% to 10.1%; vs AdaPatcher pass@1 from 5.9% to 10.1%
human_eval_details: 3 annotators (CS PhDs), 50 Defects4J bugs, pairwise forced-choice in two rounds to validate metrics; Fleiss' kappa 0.710-0.733
notes: NF dimension is patch minimality/edit locality as a proxy for review and maintenance burden; authors explicitly say it is not maintainability in full. CCR not uniformly improved (HumanEval-Java DS-Coder-6.7B CCR 71.4 under SFT vs 67.2 under PAFT). Percentages in tables are relative to Base, headline 32.6% AED reduction is relative to SFT. Contamination checked via SHA-256 of normalized snippets. Single run, no variance reported. Artifacts mentioned as released scripts/results but no URL in text.

title: ENCRUST: Encapsulated Substitution and Agentic Refinement on a Live Scaffold for Safe C-to-Rust Translation
authors: Hohyun Sim; Hyeonjoong Cho; Ali Shokri; Zhoulai Fu; Binoy Ravindran
technique_name: ENCRUST: ABI-preserving wrapper-pattern per-function translation with compile-test retry and rollback (Phase 1), type-directed wrapper elimination, and tool-equipped agentic refinement under a baseline-aware compile-and-test gate (Phase 2)
tools: C2Rust (initial unsafe transpilation); cargo build (debug/release); test-vector suites (Coreutils shell scripts; AFL++-generated inputs for Laertes); agent tools incl. find_static_mut_usages (signal-reachability analysis) and self_reflect (unsafe counts); cargo clippy for evaluation
iterations: Phase 1: up to five compile-test retries per function, then rollback to original unsafe body; Phase 2: up to 40 tool-call iterations per task (MAX_ITER = 40), task marked complete only after build + test gate passes, otherwise rollback; stall hints after five consecutive compile failures
metrics: security (memory safety): raw pointer declarations, raw pointer dereferences, unsafe lines of code, unsafe type casts, unsafe call expressions (tool-static counts, metrics from C2SaferRust); readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): Clippy warning count (tool-static); correctness: test-script / test-vector pass rate (execution) and function compilance pass rate (compiler)
benchmarks: 7 GNU Coreutils programs (C2SaferRust benchmark; 65,117 LoC, 1,210 functions, 63 test scripts) and 8 of 10 Laertes libraries (132,589 LoC, 1,156 functions, 1,000 AFL++ inputs each); 197,706 LoC and 2,366 functions in total
models: GPT-4o, closed, general instruct (temperature 0.0)
baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpiler output); C2SaferRust (with GPT-4o, temperature 0.0); EvoC2Rust (with GPT-4o, temperature 0.0); ablation Phase 1 only
effect_target_headline: Encrust reduces unsafe lines of code by 37.8% over the C2Rust baseline while achieving 100% test-vector correctness on all programs (15 programs); on Coreutils, reduces raw pointer dereferences by 55% and unsafe type casts by 60% relative to the C2Rust baseline
effect_correctness_headline: Function compilance pass rate 96.4% (Encrust) vs 66.0% (C2SaferRust) on Coreutils; Encrust achieves 100% correctness on all seven Coreutils programs and all eight Laertes libraries (EvoC2Rust 0%)
notes: Code translation (C to Rust) task; security dimension is operationalized as counts of unsafe Rust constructs (memory-safety proxy), not CWE/vulnerability scans. Clippy totals improve vs C2Rust and C2SaferRust (Coreutils 2,951 / 2,087 / 1,495; Laertes 7,174 / 7,034 / 6,453) but are worse than C2Rust for some libraries (genann 32 -> 59, lil 583 -> 698, qsort 7 -> 16, urlparser 153 -> 196), so the readability effect is mixed at program level. EvoC2Rust has lower nominal unsafe counts but does not compile (0% correctness). Correctness is 100% by construction (test-gated); EvoC2Rust safety numbers computed after substituting C2Rust bodies for missing functions. Only GPT-4o used, single deterministic run (temperature 0). Compute reported only as loop iterations (avg 21.0 per completed Phase 2 task); no tokens/cost. Laertes test vectors promised upon publication; no code URL. ACM template with placeholder venue/dates (Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 2018) - treated as preprint (arXiv 2604.04527v1). Tables are extracted as column streams but values are interpretable.

title: Record-Remix-Replay: Hierarchical GPU Kernel Optimization using Evolutionary Search
authors: Daniel Nichols; Konstantinos Parasyris; Caetano Melone; Tal Ben-Nun; Giorgis Georgakoudis; Harshitha Menon
technique_name: Record-Remix-Replay (R3): LLM-ensemble MAP-Elites evolution of kernel source with record-replay evaluation, inner Bayesian optimization (TPE) over compiler pass pipelines and launch parameters, prefix-cache-aware prompting and runtime-aware LLM selection
tools: Mneme record-replay engine built on Proteus LLVM-IR JIT; LLVM; parallel Tree Parzen Estimation (30 iterations per candidate); ROCm 7.0.2 on AMD MI300A; CUDA 12 on NVIDIA H100; vLLM for gpt-oss
iterations: 200 MAP-Elites iterations, 4 islands, population 20, migration every 20 iterations; stopping by max iterations, wall-clock time, or no-improvement window; kernels replayed K (e.g. 10) times
metrics: efficiency: kernel speedup over baseline implementation, absolute kernel time, end-to-end application speedup, compute-time reduction [execution]; search cost: time-to-solution, evaluations per hour, GPU utilization; correctness used only as a filter (bitwise or annotated-tolerance replay check), not reported as an outcome
benchmarks: HeCBench CUDA/HIP versions of Lulesh (15 kernels), MiniFE (7), S3D (54), miniWeather (7 on data path); QUDA CoarseDslash kernel case study
models: gpt-oss-120b, 120B, open, reasoning; gpt-5-mini, closed, reasoning; gpt-5, closed, reasoning (used as an ensemble)
baselines: OpenEvolve (same MAP-Elites settings and LLM ensemble); Record-Replay + Bayesian optimization over launch and compiler parameters (based on Parasyris et al. SC'23), 200 iterations; original kernel implementation
effect_target_headline: The final kernel speedup on an MI300A is 1.33×. When placed into the whole QUDA application we see a 28.4% reduction in time spent in compute
notes: Main comparative results are given as box plots (Figs 6-9) without numeric tables; headline numbers come from the QUDA case study. Correctness is a hard filter (bitwise replay check; final kernels manually verified) rather than a reported rate. Only one LLM ensemble configuration; no per-model ablation of optimization quality. Prompts not shown. Only the record-replay component (Mneme) is released; R3 'planned to be open-sourced'. No threats-to-validity section. Time-to-solution and throughput reported; no token or dollar cost.

title: Ave: Guiding Agentic GPU Optimization Using Data-Flow Invariants
authors: Hao-Hui Mai; Xiao-Yang Guo; Xiang-Yun Ding; Dai-Feng Li; Qiu-Chun Yu; Chen-Zhun Guo
venue: Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 32nd Symposium on Operating Systems Principles
technique_name: Ave: tile-based DSL with tag functions/assertions checked by compile-time SMT-backed static analysis, ICRL (text-gradient) planner over an expert knowledge base, and a lowering agent, iterating with unit tests and runtime profiling
tools: Ave compiler (MLIR, LLVM 20 AMDGPU backend extensions, ROCm 7.2.2), Z3 SMT solver; Codex harness runtime; latency profiling (1 s warm-up, mean over at least 100 runs); CUDA 12.8 for H200
iterations: Up to ten optimization trials (rounds) per workload, keeping the fastest valid candidate; only a measured speedup replaces the current kernel; KernelBench generation stops at first test-passing candidate (pass@1/3)
metrics: efficiency: normalized effective throughput (geometric mean) vs hipBLASLt/AITER/PyTorch reference, effective TFLOPS, count of tasks above parity [execution]; correctness: compilation, invariant checks, unit tests, manual reward-hacking review, pass@1/3, optimization success [execution]
benchmarks: Production kernels on AMD MI300X: BF16 square GEMM, causal GQA flash attention, fused MoE (FP8), five configurations each; same on NVIDIA H200; KernelBench Level 1 (100 tasks) and Level 2 (100 tasks); 60 selected KernelBench GEMM/convolution tasks for invariant ablation
languages: Ave Pythonic tile-based DSL (GPU kernels; AMD CDNA3/CDNA4, NVIDIA Hopper)
models: GPT-5.6 Sol (closed); DeepSeek V4 Pro (open); DeepSeek V4 Flash (open)
baselines: Agentic frameworks KernelFalcon, KSearch, CUDAForge, Atrex; expert libraries hipBLASLt, AITER, HipKittens, ROCm Triton (cuBLASLt, FlashAttention-3 fork, DeepGEMM fork on H200); ablations without ICRL, without invariants, runtime feedback only
effect_target_headline: With GPT-5.6 Sol, its optimized kernels achieve 89–99% of the effective throughput of state-of-the-art hand-optimized libraries and improve geometric-mean throughput by 1.62–1176× over uncontaminated agentic baselines (AMD MI300X, GEMM/flash attention/MoE)
effect_correctness_headline: On 200 KernelBench tasks, with GPT-5.6 Sol and in-context DSL examples, Ave produces valid kernels within three attempts for 100% of Level 1 and 88% of Level 2 problems; invariants improve success in every dataset–model pair (Table 4)
notes: Tables 1, 3, 4 and Figure 2/3 are garbled in extraction (cost/turn/token columns misaligned). Contamination considered via 'uncontaminated agentic baselines' (Atrex copies AITER reference kernel) and a DSL absent from training corpora; manual reward-hacking review. Ablation (flash attention): full Ave 588 TFLOPS vs 190/255/194 for ablated harnesses. Best-of-trials reporting; no variance across agent runs; limitations discussed in Discussion but no formal threats section.

title: Xe-Forge: Multi-Stage LLM-Powered Kernel Optimization for Intel GPU
authors: Marcin Spoczynski; Daniel Fleischer; Moshe Berchansky; Gabriel Stan; Shira Guskin; Weilin Xu
technique_name: Xe-Forge: LLM-planned multi-stage optimization pipeline with Chain-of-Verification-and-Refinement (CoVeR) agents and Intel GPU knowledge base

iterations: Not a generation-time loop. Data selection is one pass per candidate example with thresholds ACJ >= Trivial and AQJ >= Acceptable; training is 3 epochs with loss masked to assistant trajectory tokens only. Inference uses OpenHands with max 300 turns per instance, pass@1.
metrics: readability-maintainability (architectural conformance / structural quality): distribution of AQJ four-tier verdicts over all generated patches - High, High-with-concerns (HWC), Acceptable, Low - produced by a repository- and issue-specific rubric with priority-ordered axes and prose anchors [llm-judge]; the ACJ five-level complexity verdict (Trivial/Low/Moderate/High/Expert over five axes) is used for data selection, not as an outcome [llm-judge]. correctness: SWE-bench resolved rate under pass@1 (all specified unit tests pass on first attempt) [execution]; patch precision = resolved issues / patches generated [execution]. Convergent validity: Spearman correlation of the judge verdicts against 157 static architecture metrics [tool-static].
benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (500 verified bug-fixing instances) and SWE-bench Multilingual (300 bug-fixing instances across 9 non-Python languages). Training pool: 5,000 high-quality Python trajectories from RepoForge, filtered to 3,360 architecturally curated instances; the metric-based filtering baseline yields 1,548 instances. Stated to have no overlap between training and evaluation data.
languages: Python for training; evaluation additionally covers 9 non-Python languages via SWE-bench Multilingual (e.g., Ruby, Java)
models: Fine-tuned: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B (open-weights, instruct/reasoning). Teacher for trajectory generation: MiniMax-M2.5 (open-weights). Judge backbone: described only as 'a strong LLM' and never identified.
baselines: Original (base model, no fine-tuning); FullData (fine-tuned on the entire 5,000-trajectory pool, i.e. unfiltered SFT); Metrics (filtering by thresholded static architecture metrics, Qwen3-8B only); for the judge itself, random-forest prediction of ACJ/AQJ verdicts from 157 static metrics.
effect_target_headline: "our approach increases the proportion of architecturally conformant patches from 61-72% to 84-94% across model sizes" (abstract/introduction); per model, "For Qwen3-8B, the combined High+HWC proportion increases from 60.9% to 83.6%; for Qwen3-14B, from 64.0% to 87.1%; and for Qwen3-32B, from 72.1% to 93.5%." Versus the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural quality is only comparable: "High+HWC proportions of 83.6% vs. 87.5% on Qwen3-8B, 87.1% vs. 83.9% on Qwen3-14B, and 93.5% vs. 93.3% on Qwen3-32B".
effect_correctness_headline: "Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B/14B/32B on 3,360 curated instances achieves resolved rates of up to 27.2% on SWE-bench Verified - up to 540% over the base model and 256% over unfiltered fine-tuning." Per model on SWE-bench Verified: 3.2% -> 17.4% (Qwen3-8B), 4.6% -> 17.8% (Qwen3-14B), 9.0% -> 27.2% (Qwen3-32B) versus Original; 6.8% -> 17.4%, 9.4% -> 17.8%, 15.6% -> 27.2% versus FullData. SWE-bench Multilingual: "our approach improves over the Original baseline by 286% - 420%" (1.4% -> 4.0%, 4.3% -> 9.7%, 3.3% -> 14%). Metric-based filtering baseline: 14.4% vs 17.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 4.7% vs 6.7% on Multilingual (Qwen3-8B).
notes: Main methodological concern for a reviewer: the architectural-quality outcome is measured by AQJ, the same author-built LLM judge that was used to select the training data, so the headline NF improvement is partly circular; the judge is never validated against human expert ratings (only against static metrics, where it deliberately does not correlate), and the LLM backbone powering the judges is nowhere identified. Against the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural-conformance gain essentially disappears (83.6 vs 87.5, 87.1 vs 83.9, 93.5 vs 93.3), so the clear NF gain is only versus the untuned base model; the paper's distinctive claim versus FullData is about resolved rate and data efficiency, not conformance. Table 1 is hard to read because the AQJ columns are reported as relative changes to each model's own baseline while the baseline row is absolute, and the extraction garbles one cell ('17,1' for 17.1). Internal inconsistencies to check: the abstract says 286-424% cross-language improvement while Section 5.2 says 286-420%; Section 5.1 says 'improves the resolved rate by 174% - 256% compared to using the full dataset' where those figures are ratios rather than percentage improvements; Table 3's first row is labelled 'Original' with size 5,000 and value 6.8%, which is the FullData condition in Table 1, not the untuned base model; Table 3 lists SWE-Multi 5.0% for that row while Table 2 gives FullData Qwen3-8B as 3.0%. Tables 4 and 5 appear to have their captions swapped relative to their contents (the 'ACJ-style' table uses AQJ-correlated features). Results are single pass@1 runs with no variance, repeated runs or statistical tests, and no compute/cost figures despite the paper itself noting the token cost of agentic judging.

title: From C to Idiomatic Rust: A Ship-of-Theseus Agentic Translation
authors: V. Sartakov
venue: Proceedings of the 2nd International Workshop on AI for Software Modernization
technique_name: Ship-of-Theseus agentic C-to-Rust migration: c2rust lossless baseline, leaf-first call-graph ordering, per-function LLM reimplementation, two hard gates (Gate A compilation plus idiomaticity criteria, Gate B runtime behavioural equivalence with trace-divergence feedback), split into Phase 1 (signatures and bodies) and Phase 2 (global mutable state)
tools: c2rust transpiler (Clang AST based); Clang/LLVM; the Rust compiler; static call-graph analysis for leaf-based ordering; equivalent trace instrumentation of old and new implementations for divergence diagnosis; end-to-end runtime validation with a public DNS resolver, curl download and netperf through the tunnel, plus a wire-format integration test; OpenCode-based agent infrastructure enhanced by 'rtk' and 'OAC' (neither explained); no version numbers given for any tool
iterations: Per function, the agent proposes an implementation, compiles it, runs the runtime tests and revises from compiler errors or trace divergence, repeating until Gate A and Gate B both pass, with reversion to the last verified state where needed; no maximum iteration count is stated. Phase 2 requires one global at a time with full runtime tests after each wrapping. The whole migration spanned about 45 commits (each porting one to ten functions) and 37 developer-hours over four working days
metrics: security (memory safety): SAFE% = 100(1 - (EX+NM)/(EX0+NM0)) where EX counts unsafe extern "C" fn declarations and NM counts #[no_mangle] annotations; RUST% = 100(1 - (PA+DU)/(PA0+DU0)) where PA counts raw pointer arithmetic sites and DU counts deep unsafe operations such as copy_nonoverlapping and write_bytes; also absolute counts of static mut globals wrapped and of unsafe blocks [all tool-static source counting]. readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): the five criteria C1 zero unsafe in function signatures, C2 slice-based buffer access, C3 no static mut, C4 no extern "C" on internal functions, C5 no C string or memory functions, enforced as hard errors at Gate A [tool-static]; SLOC of the resulting codebase. Correctness: compilation plus end-to-end behavioural equivalence (same output and state modification for the same input), checked after every port [execution]
benchmarks: Single case study, no benchmark suite: iodine, a production-quality DNS tunnel of approximately 12.5 kSLOC of C across 17 source files, with 168 functions ported and 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server). c2rust baseline counts: 178 EX, 73 NM, 319 PA, 144 DU
models: Not properly reported. The paper states translation was performed 'using subscription-based plans and the OpenCode-based infrastructure' and that 'the best result (fewest iterations) was achieved with Qwen3.6-27B'; no other model is named, no sizes or open/closed status for the others, and no per-model results are given. ChatGPT and Copilot are acknowledged only for proofreading the manuscript
baselines: The c2rust transpiler output (mechanically translated, non-idiomatic Rust) serves as the baseline against which SAFE% and RUST% are defined. No comparison against direct LLM C-to-Rust translation (the approach the paper argues against) and no comparison against other migration tools
effect_target_headline: Server porting (commits 1-31) lifts SAFE% to 72% and RUST% to 47%; client porting (commits 32-41) completes all 168 signatures at SAFE%=95%; static-mut elimination (commits 39-45, extending to the end of history) wraps the 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server) in atomics or mutexes, lifting RUST% to its final 57%. The final codebase is approximately 10.3 kSLOC of idiomatic Rust across 16 files, translated from an original 12.5 kSLOC C codebase, with no unsafe extern "C" function declarations and no static mut left in the evaluated code. Client porting and static-mut elimination cut the client's unsafe blocks from roughly 86 to 40. Residual gap: five signal-handler EX type aliases and six #[no_mangle] entry-point annotations, and 99 PA and 99 DU uses confined to FFI boundary adapters
effect_correctness_headline: Functional equivalence was verified end-to-end: after each of the 168 function ports and each of the 37 static mut wrappings (16 client, 21 server), Gate B ran the tunnel against the public resolver under real traffic for 30 s or more, verified curl download and netperf through the tunnel, and passed a wire-format integration test
notes: ELIGIBILITY NOTE: this is a translation/migration paper, so a reviewer could route it to the 'adjacent' side list (LLM refactoring of human-written code, EC4). It was included because the evaluated artifact is new Rust code that the LLM wrote (from a C source and a transpiled baseline), the five idiomaticity criteria and the safety counts are explicitly non-functional properties of that generated code, and the technique is an intervention (an agentic compile-plus-runtime feedback loop) designed to improve them. Other caveats. (1) The models are essentially unreported: only Qwen3.6-27B is named, as the one needing fewest iterations, and the claim that 'a particular model choice does not materially affect the outcome' is asserted without any supporting data. The agent tooling 'rtk' and 'OAC' is named but never explained or cited. (2) Single case study on one 12.5 kSLOC program; no repeated runs, no variance, no statistical test, and no comparison against the direct-LLM-translation baseline the paper argues against. (3) SAFE% and RUST% are author-defined composite metrics; they deliberately omit the raw unsafe count (justified as not penalising correct refactoring), and the headline 'no unsafe extern "C" function declarations' sits slightly in tension with SAFE% = 95% (the residual is five signal-handler EX type aliases plus six #[no_mangle] annotations). (4) Correctness is verified thoroughly but qualitatively; no pass rate or test-count figure is given, and the runtime oracle depends on a live public DNS resolver, which is not a reproducible test environment. (5) Notable negative finding worth recording: batching three Mutex wrappings produced a live deadlock that compiled and passed static checks but stalled transfers at zero bytes, and POSIX getopt() externs (optarg, optind, opterr, optopt) were found to be unwrappable and were deferred. (6) The process is explicitly human-in-the-loop: type deduplication, FFI adapter scaffolding and lock-wrapping orchestration were handled by a human as exceptions, so the 37 developer-hours figure mixes agent and human effort. (7) No artifact release; the only URL is upstream iodine (https://code.kryo.se/iodine/). (8) No contamination discussion, despite iodine being a long-standing public open-source project. (9) Figures 1, 2 and 3 extracted poorly (the three-column code listing in Figure 1 and the metric plot in Figure 3 are interleaved), but all quoted numbers come from the running text of Section 4.3 and the Validation paragraph.

title: Specification Before Generation: A Pre-Registered, Five-Model Paired Evaluation of a Specification Frame for LLM-Generated Code in Money, Time, Idempotency, and Access Tasks
authors: Sandeep Dhuri
technique_name: Specification Frame (fixed, task-agnostic 267-word specification preamble with Role/Context/Task/Constraints sections, prepended inline to every task prompt)
tools: Scoring instruments (not part of the technique): nine deterministic AST-based checkers written by the author (money_float, exact_compare, naive_datetime, sql_param, open_redirect, path_traversal, hardcoded_secret, password_hash, idempotency_key), validated with an 11-bad/11-good unit fixture gauntlet and 50 per-task fixture proofs; Bandit 1.9.4 as an instrument-blind secondary scanner; exploratory Python byte-compilation check.

metrics: security: number of registered defect-class checkers that fired per output (0-5), from nine deterministic AST/regex checkers mapped to CWE-682, CWE-697, CWE-89, CWE-601, CWE-22, CWE-798, CWE-916/CWE-328 plus two domain rules with no CWE [tool-static]; Bandit 1.9.4 medium-or-high severity findings per output [tool-static]; manual adjudication of a seeded 10 percent sample of findings [human]. benchmarks: 50 author-written realistic backend tasks in four regulated domains (money MO01-MO12 = 12 tasks, idempotency ID01-ID12 = 12, date/time DA01-DA10 + DT11-DT12 = 12, authentication/access AU01-AU14 = 14), with 106 checker registrations, 11-13 per checker; 100 prompts (bare and frame arms) and 500 outputs. Not a public benchmark; all materials deposited on Zenodo.
models: claude-sonnet-5 (Anthropic, closed, flagship); gpt-5.6-sol (OpenAI, closed, flagship successor used on run day); gemini-3.1-pro-preview (Google, closed); deepseek-v4-pro (DeepSeek, open-weight lineage, hosted); qwen/qwen3.8-27b (Alibaba/Qwen, 27B, open-weight, hosted on Groq). Temperature 0 requested; two endpoints (Anthropic, OpenAI) do not accept the parameter and ran at provider default.
baselines: Paired bare arm: the identical task text with no preamble and no system message, same model and request parameters, two consecutive stateless calls per task. No length-matched neutral preamble and no reason-first control were run (acknowledged as an unexcluded confound).
effect_target_headline: "The frame reduced defects in all five models (mean reduction 0.16 to 0.70 findings per task, every Holm-adjusted sign test significant, every bootstrap confidence interval excluding zero). Where the arms differed, the frame arm won 95 of 100 times. It never made any model worse in any domain." Pooled (descriptive only): "the frame arm carried 23 findings against 148 in the bare arm, an 84 percent reduction in the named defect classes" across 250 pairs. Per model mean delta: claude-sonnet-5 0.68 [0.38, 1.02]; deepseek-v4-pro 0.40 [0.24, 0.58]; gemini-3.1-pro-preview 0.70 [0.38, 1.08]; qwen3.8-27b 0.56 [0.36, 0.76]; gpt-5.6-sol 0.16 [0.04, 0.28]. Independent scanner: "Bandit found 53 medium-or-high issues in the bare arm and 11 in the frame arm, in the same direction for every model."
human_eval_details: One annotator (the author). A pre-registered seeded 10 percent sample of 18 checker findings (seed 20260905) was adjudicated against a strict true-positive standard; all 18 were true positives. No inter-rater agreement is reported because there is only one rater.
artifact_url: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22850887 (dataset v1.1; v1.0 = 10.5281/zenodo.22598205); frame introduced in the author's book, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21584309
notes: Unusually transparent study: pre-registered with four dated addenda, a one-shot no-regeneration rule, a full deviations section, and all 500 outputs plus checkers and analysis code deposited under a DOI. Caveats a reviewer should weigh: (1) functional correctness was explicitly NOT measured (only an exploratory byte-compilation check: 247/250 bare and 236/250 frame compile, with 14 of the 14 frame failures being transport-truncated files), so a correctness/security trade-off of the kind RealSec-bench and Dai et al. report cannot be ruled out; (2) the author designed both the frame and the nine checkers and wrote the book that introduced the frame (declared as a competing interest), with Bandit as the instrument-blind corroboration; (3) 16 of 500 outputs were truncated in transport, 14 of them frame-arm, which the author notes can only bias toward the frame, and a sensitivity analysis excluding those pairs is reported and preserves every per-model conclusion; (4) one run per arm, so within-model variance is unmeasured; (5) two providers would not accept temperature 0. Dimension assignment is slightly borderline: four of the nine measured defect classes (money float arithmetic, float money equality, naive datetimes, missing idempotency) are domain-correctness rules with weak or no CWE mapping, while five are standard CWE security classes; the paper itself frames all nine as security-adjacent defect classes and Bandit corroborates only the CWE subset. Training-data contamination is never discussed (tasks are author-written and unpublished before the run, which mitigates it incidentally). Tables IV and V survived extraction mostly intact but the column-to-row alignment in Table IV is scrambled; the per-model numbers above were reconstructed from the column order given in the header and should be spot-checked.

title: Groupwise Agentic Grading and Advantage Redistribution for Code Agent RL
